title: Backup Delivery Plane for Offline Asset Access

context.problem_statement: When the Seneca.js backend server goes down (planned maintenance, infrastructure failure, network issues), tablet/field users lose all access to asset data. There is currently no offline fallback or backup delivery mechanism. This creates a single point of failure for field operations that depend on asset data.

options: Backup Delivery Plane: S3 + presigned URLs + Kinde JWT + Lambda Signer (chosen)
DynamoDB Global Tables with direct client read access
CloudFront signed URLs without Lambda authorization
Service Worker with full Seneca API caching
Static JSON export to S3 on a schedule (no auth, public bucket)
GraphQL persisted queries with offline cache (Apollo)
outcome: Build a separate Backup Delivery Plane independent from the Seneca backend. Encrypted asset bundles are generated periodically by a Builder Lambda (reading DynamoDB directly), stored in private S3 with per-tenant key prefixes, and delivered to authenticated clients via short-lived presigned URLs generated by a Signer Lambda. Authentication uses existing Kinde JWTs verified by a Lambda Authorizer at API Gateway. Clients cache bundles locally in IndexedDB (encrypted at rest) and fall back to cached data when both Seneca and the backup plane are unreachable.
rationale: This approach provides maximum independence from the main Seneca server while reusing the existing Kinde authentication investment (DEC-000005). No AWS credentials are exposed to client devices. Per-tenant S3 prefixes combined with IAM policies and JWT tenant claim validation provide strong multi-tenant isolation. Versioned bundles with pointer files enable safe rollback. The architecture uses only serverless AWS primitives (Lambda, S3, KMS, API Gateway, EventBridge) keeping operational overhead low and costs proportional to usage. Alternative approaches were rejected: DynamoDB Global Tables require AWS credentials on clients; CloudFront signed URLs lack flexible per-request authorization; Service Worker caching couples to the Seneca API surface; static public S3 exports have no authentication; GraphQL offline requires a fundamentally different API layer.

risk.acceptance: Introduces new infrastructure (3 Lambdas, S3 bucket, KMS keys, API Gateway endpoint) that must be maintained independently. Bundle staleness is bounded by cron frequency (default 60 min). KMS key management adds operational complexity. IndexedDB caching on tablets is greenfield work with no existing offline infrastructure in the codebase. Acceptable tradeoffs given the critical business need for field operation continuity.

security_considerations: No Public S3 Access: Bucket uses Block Public Access; all reads via presigned URLs only
No AWS Credentials on Client: Tablet app never holds IAM keys; uses presigned URLs for download
JWT Authentication: Every backup request requires a valid Kinde JWT verified by Lambda Authorizer
Tenant Isolation: S3 prefix scheme (tenant/{tenantId}/) + JWT tenant claim validation prevents cross-tenant access
Encryption at Rest: S3 SSE-KMS with per-tenant Customer Managed Keys
Encryption in Transit: HTTPS required for presigned URLs and API Gateway
Short-lived URLs: Presigned URLs expire in 60-300 seconds, minimising exposure window
Bundle Integrity: SHA-256 hash verified by client before decryption
Local Encryption: IndexedDB cached bundles encrypted at rest on device
Key Rotation: KMS automatic key rotation enabled; presigned URLs are ephemeral
Tenant Claim Validation: JWT org_code/org_id claim cross-referenced against allowlist, never trusted alone

bundle_generation.description: Periodic Lambda reads DynamoDB entities and produces encrypted bundles in S3
bundle_generation.flow: EventBridge (cron) → Builder Lambda → DynamoDB (read pqs/asset, pqs/sap, pqs/group) → ZIP → KMS encrypt → S3 upload → latest.json update

bundle_delivery.description: Authenticated endpoint returns a short-lived presigned URL for the latest bundle
bundle_delivery.flow: Client → Kinde JWT → API Gateway → JWT Authorizer Lambda → Signer Lambda → S3 presigned URL → Client downloads
bundle_delivery.response: { url, expiresAt, bundleId, sha256, sequenceNum, validUntil }

client_caching.description: Frontend caches bundles in IndexedDB with encrypted-at-rest storage
client_caching.flow: Download bundle → Verify SHA-256 → Decrypt → Store in IndexedDB → Serve from cache when offline
client_caching.fallback: Last-known-good cached bundle with validUntil expiry and degraded-mode warning

alternatives_analysis.option: DynamoDB Global Tables with direct client read
alternatives_analysis.pros: Real-time data, AWS-managed replication, no bundle generation needed
alternatives_analysis.cons: Requires AWS IAM credentials on client devices (unacceptable security risk), no offline support, expensive at scale
alternatives_analysis.rejected_reason: Violates 'no AWS keys in app' requirement

alternatives_analysis.pros: Lower latency via CDN edge, no Lambda cold starts, simpler architecture
alternatives_analysis.cons: CloudFront key pair management less flexible than Lambda, harder to add per-request tenant validation, key pair rotation more complex
alternatives_analysis.rejected_reason: Insufficient authorization flexibility for multi-tenant per-request validation

alternatives_analysis.option: Service Worker with full Seneca API caching
alternatives_analysis.pros: Transparent to app code, caches all API responses, progressive enhancement
alternatives_analysis.cons: Couples to Seneca API surface (defeats purpose of independence), complex cache invalidation, doesn't work when Seneca changes API
alternatives_analysis.rejected_reason: Creates dependency on Seneca API availability for cache population

alternatives_analysis.option: Static JSON export to public S3
alternatives_analysis.pros: Simplest implementation, no auth needed, fast CDN delivery
alternatives_analysis.cons: No authentication, no tenant isolation, public data exposure
alternatives_analysis.rejected_reason: Completely unacceptable security posture for tenant asset data

alternatives_analysis.option: GraphQL persisted queries with Apollo offline cache
alternatives_analysis.pros: Rich offline support, automatic sync, mature tooling
alternatives_analysis.cons: Requires fundamentally different API layer (not Seneca patterns), heavy client dependency, vendor lock-in to Apollo
alternatives_analysis.rejected_reason: Architectural mismatch with Seneca pattern-based backend (DEC-000007)
